title: The questionable allure of Emerald Fennell's style over substance.

commenti.body:
You really think that’s all those movies are about, particularly Promising Young Woman?

I presume you are a man; I am too. But I have talked to *so many* women for whom PYW was the first time they felt really seen by a film touching on those topics. So much so that I went with a female friend to Saltburn on the weekend and she told me that she couldn’t even finish Promising because it was so triggering of experiences she’d had in her past.

Promsing in particular has a power that transcends just the aesthetic and - I personally feel - completely artificial ending that is way too pat and convenient to feel real. (I had similar issues with the ending of Saltburn.) But I think it’s somewhat ignorant to deny it’s not just an important film for women, but a timely one as well. It put date rape/predatory male behaviour in a populist film in a way that has never really been done before. Tying it all up neatly in a feminist revenge fantasy at the end was a misstep in my opinion, but the catharsis was much needed for many of the women I’ve spoken to about it.

And to me, Saltburn isn’t just about rich people having nice things or being vapid or what people will do to get there. It’s about the psychosexual power dynamics between the haves and the have nots, the artificiality and emotional avoidance of British politeness and class constructs, of repressed sexuality and the fetishisation of the image and idea of the young and the beautiful.

It’s not a truly great film in my mind and it gets way too silly and unbelievable at the end for my liking, but I can still appreciate the way it confronts ideas not too dissimilar to Parasite did, but through a much different social lens because of the culture differences.

I’ve seen quite a few people with this opinion but I got a totally different read on the movie. I think first it deals with obsession. Obsession with people. Obsession with wealth. Obsession with tradition. And how those obsessions play out in our cast of characters. I think it was brilliant to have Oliver be from a wealthy upper middle class family. The audience, like Felix, were supposed to really feel for this poor boy trying his best to fit in and just only being able to be a weirdo and outsider despite his best efforts. We, like Felix, excused his behavior because of his false upbringing. But truthfully he grew up in a loving home and probably never wanted for anything himself. That somehow was not enough for him. He still wants more. More money. More power. I think the movie shows the gulf between the generational wealth and middle class in Britain. One gets you an entire castle and estate. The other you are living nice in the suburbs. But it’s no castle. Which is what motivates Oliver. He wants the castle. Whether an actual castle or Felix at first. He wants it. And when he is found out by Felix he goes about getting his wants satisfied a different way. It really adds a disturbing level of conniving to Oliver’s character. So I think there’s plenty to think on about contemporary messaging but also I think it’s an interesting movie about this really disturbed individual who himself isn’t happy at the level of wealth he is limited to due to his class. Which doesn’t make him a hero. There are none. He’s not Robin Hood trying to steal for the rich and give to the poor. He’s like most of the other upper middle class dudes trying to break into the next strata of wealth they don’t need. Selfish and sadistic.

i disagree with both your premise and your conclusion. 

Style IS substance. Both Promising Young Woman and Saltburn are movies that evoke strong emotions— look at the reactions the bathtub scene is getting on TikTok lol. Their purpose is to make you feel something. They’re parables and parallels and expressions and stylized depictions of real life experiences. 

In PYW, rape culture is shown as it really is— inescapable and pervasive. Even Bo Burnham’s character, who is presented as a nice sweet guy, is a skeeve. It’s not about taking down one bad dude, it’s about a woman fighting a losing battle. 

Saltburn is about capitalism, and the lengths that people will go to social climb. The “twist ending” that it was planned all along isn’t meant to just shock you, it’s to show that from the moment you decide you want that kind wealth you’ve already lost your humanity.

A movie doesn’t have to have a new, deep, layered, insightful thesis to be good. A simple theme with good craft is usually the best way of communicating a message

“It’s about the psychosexual power dynamics of the haves and the have nots.”

I think you’re giving Saltburn quite a bit more credit than it deserves. Mainly since, Oliver isn’t a “have not.” He’s a “have less than.” In fact, it seems he still “has” a good bit from where he comes from.

There are elements of some of those other things you listed, but it doesn’t explore any of that. The only thing the film has to say in the end is “obscene wealth is so alluring that the middle-class would be willing to do anything for it, because being middle-class is just so BORING!”

It’s a film devoid of anything beneath its surface.

Just because you don't see the substance doesn't mean its not there. In PYW, there's no triumph in her death or in the ways she hurts people. Men are the ones who believe justice can be found through violence. It's a story they tell over and over again. But in PYW the main character is aware of how diminished her anger's made her. It feels terrible, and in the end it destroys her. That's not a victory. Yes, the gift the filmmmaker gives her audience is the fairytale of having the rapist/murderer arrested, but it comes with the assurance that the nice guy will always be a coward. And it's also a reminder that the arrest is only possible with the help of the one person who actually took accountability for their complicity and sought redemption. And, as the film shows us, he is rare.

And Saltburn is not about material wealth or even envy. It's about exposing the toxic way the "kindness" of the rich always comes with strings attached. Know your place. Mind your manners. Don't get ideas. Just play by our rules and in the end, we'll use you up and throw you out when we're done with you. The family doesn't see Oliver, as the poor boy they believe him to be, as a real person. To them, he's a puppet. A plaything to serve their needs--emotional, sexual, social--until he doesn't.

Therefore, it's a story that asks if what Oliver does to them is any different or worse than what they are willing to do to him. He turns out to be the puppet master, who is first drawn to Felix for sexual and social reasons. But when he can't have this, he disposes of his puppets without a care, the same way the family disposed of Pam and Farleigh's mother and all the other Olivers of summers past. Is he the villain? Or is he just like them?

I agree with you and think the other commenters are drawing links where they don't exist (having watched saltburn, not PYW so can't comment on it) the film tries to say a lot (and could have, if the plot had gone a different way, I think the first half was brilliant) but trips over it's grand ambitions to have a conclusive and shocking ending, and ends up saying nothing at all

>Both Promising Young Woman and Saltburn are movies that evoke strong emotions— look at the reactions the bathtub scene is getting on TikTok lol. Their purpose is to make you feel something. They’re parables and parallels and expressions and stylized depictions of real life experiences.

Just because people find the bathtub scene outrageous doesn't mean it has any depth or merit beyond trying to scandalize people.

Promising Young Woman: many more people are complicit in rape culture than just the rapist. Society turns a blind eye to what a sexual abused woman goes through, and the rapist is often not punished.

Saltburn: The British class system is largely based on lineage, not money. There is no way for Oliver to be apart of the same class as the Cattons, as the father is a Sir of some type. Farleigh's speech about how Oliver doesn't belong at Saltburn and can never be one of them alludes to this. We learn Oliver isn't actually poor like he claimed to be, yet he'll never be apart of that upper class like Felix cause you need to be born into it. So, he tries to "replace" Felix and eventually ends up >!killing off the rest of the family aside from the father and taking their spot in the upper class by taking over Saltburn.!<

These are the "bigger" messages I've gotten from them. Art is subjective in that we all take different meanings out of it. I think she is making fun films that are nice to look at and that's totally fine. But there are definitely some deeper messages there if you listen to a lot of the dialogue.

Right, but i'm uncomfortable with villainizing a middle class character as this deranged usurper. If anything paranoia and distrust should be directed at the 1% and not the middle class. Fennell uses pop culture like Superbad, Bloc Party and aughts fashion, so clearly the story is set in the real world. And in the real world, it's a small group at the top who have all the power.

I appreciate your explanations of Saltburn. But for PYW the scenes of the delayed text messages to the villains, and the smiley face from Cassie, really seems like an intentional, triumphant gotcha moment. The upbeat vibes of the arrest scenes don't seem to be trying to portray bleakness or hopelessness. Everything in the mise-en-scene to me points to: she got even. But really, she didn't (Nina and Cassie are both dead now).

Ehh anyone can be a villain regardless of class or the social messaging we would prefer. Plus it’s not like the rich are portrayed kindly. They are portrayed as cold self centered people. Felix takes on a poor pet every year to make himself feel better about a disconnecting amount of wealth. But he and the rest of his family are still disconnected. They inhabit another realm entirely and don’t seem to care about anyone but themselves. Look what happens with their friend Pamela. She supposedly stayed with the family for quite a spell then they kicked her out in the middle of the night and next you hear she has been murdered by her ex like she was afraid she would be. Rosamund Pike’s character is unbothered though and think it’s just another way Pamela is trying to bother her. While Oliver is truly an outright obvious villain I would say Felix’s family has that banality of evil going on. The disconnect from society they experience due to their extreme wealth makes them incredibly anti social and not able to mix with society at large.

The British class structure is different than the one I come from, the American. I’ve heard Brits have an OWNING class, because they have had portions of the country in their family for ages. There is a very real difference between being part of the OWNING class like Elordi’s character, and being part of an upper middle class like Keoghan’s character. That nuance is tailored to a specific audience and I wasn’t even aware of it until I did a lot of digging around for that film

I think Emerald Fennel simply knows how to get people talking about her movies. She is obviously well-versed enough to start making logical, sound points, but then she intentionally sabotages that point in such an egregious way that it illicit reactions from people. And the fact she has done the specific thing to get people riled up multiple times in her movies means it’s not on accident. She knows exactly which point to fuck up to have the greatest effect. This also demonstrates a strong grasp on the subject in a way. 

She’s a cringy edgelord but a really good one.

That doesn’t make the film any more poignant in my opinion. If her message is that it has to be taken, not given, then my question is: so what? Because luxurious wealth is better than comfortable wealth? It doesn’t convey the stakes of their class difference at all. 

What would’ve been interesting is if she went deeper into Keoghan’s character, exploring what kind of person it takes to break through that class barrier (i.e., a psychopath) and what that says about England as a whole. But again, she never meaningfully goes there.
It paints a picture of the people who want it, and those who have it. Whether you’re interested in that sort of discourse is totally personal opinion. But it IS saying something about it.
Okay, so what is it saying?

It’s not that deep bro

Seriously though, I think of it more as an uncomfortably fun movie that touches on the juxtaposition between middle upper class and this “owning” class. Key word “touches” - it does not need to dive deep. Not everything requires depth and this movie was not trying to do that - at least in my opinion. 

Let it just be a movie that tricks the viewer and instead leads them down one man’s quest for complete domination. It was fun, beautifully shot, fantastic soundtrack and A+ acting. 8/10

I’ll also add to back up point as fun movie. They bloody revealed all his sinful acts at the end anyway - it pissed me off admiringly at first to assume me as the viewer couldn’t piece it together. But I think now they were just having fun with it
It’s definitely fun. I enjoyed it, just left the ending a bit wanting. It’s been the most interesting movie to discuss so far this season.

It’s definitely fun. I enjoyed it, just left the ending a bit wanting. 

It’s been the most interesting movie to discuss/read about so far this season to me.

I quite like dark & light elements together. Give me brutal cynicism with a happy-go-lucky pop track anytime. Cassie and Nina ultimately lost everything. Whereas Al, Ryan, Joe appeared to gain it all. In her spitefully played out ending, she got her truth heard, and Al's medical license. True justice was never possible when you've been robbed of what your life could have been. In her head, she dies a martyr to her friend, which is how she had been living until she briefly found happiness and became utterly disillusioned once more.
